title: Prompting power
content_html:
What We're Doing

In this lesson, students discover that getting good results from an AI chatbot like ChatGPT is a skill — not luck. Many first-time users type short, vague requests and get disappointing answers, then conclude "the AI is bad." Today's activity flips that idea on its head: students will run the same request three times, making it more specific each time, and watch the AI's answers transform from generic to genuinely useful.

By the end of the session, students will have created a personal "Prompt Recipe Card" — a simple reusable formula for writing clear prompts — and used it to solve a real request of their own choosing (e.g. a birthday party idea, a study plan, a story). The core takeaway: the quality of your question shapes the quality of the AI's answer.

Tools & Resources

  • ChatGPT (free tier) — https://chat.openai.com. Requires an account (email or Google sign-in). Free tier uses GPT-3.5/GPT-4o-mini depending on availability; may show "busy" messages at peak times — have students refresh or wait 30 seconds.
  • Alternative if ChatGPT access is limited: Microsoft Copilot — https://copilot.microsoft.com (free, no login required for basic chat on some regions) or Google Gemini — https://gemini.google.com.
  • Printed or digital Prompt Recipe Card template (teacher to prepare — a simple table with columns: Task / Role / Detail / Format).
  • Shared class document (Google Doc or physical flipchart) to collect students' "before and after" prompts for comparison.
  • Free-tier watch-outs: message limits during high traffic, occasional login/verification prompts, and slower response times when many devices are on the same Wi-Fi network — test connectivity beforehand.

Step-by-Step Activity

  1. Open with a quick poll: ask students to guess what happens if you ask ChatGPT "Tell me about dogs" versus a very specific question. Write both guesses on the board.
  2. Have every student open ChatGPT (or the alternative tool) and type this exact vague prompt: Tell me about dogs. Let them read the response silently for 1 minute.
  3. As a class, discuss: Is this answer useful? What's missing? Who is it "for"? (It's generic — not written for anyone in particular.)
  4. Introduce the 4-part Prompt Recipe: Role (who should the AI act as?), Task (what exactly do you want?), Detail (context, audience, constraints), Format (list, story, table, short paragraph).
  5. Model rewriting the dog prompt live using the recipe: You are a vet. Explain to a curious 10-year-old why dogs wag their tails, in 3 fun facts with emojis. Run it and compare the output to the first attempt.
  6. Students rewrite their own version of the dog prompt using the recipe and run it. Ask 2–3 volunteers to read their prompt and result aloud.
  7. Now students choose their own topic (a hobby, a school subject, a problem they have) and write a Level 1 prompt (vague, one sentence) and run it.
  8. Students then write a Level 2 prompt on the same topic using the 4-part recipe, and run it.
  9. Students write a Level 3 prompt adding one more constraint (word limit, tone, or example format) to push the answer further, and run it.
  10. Students fill in their Prompt Recipe Card with their best Level 3 prompt and paste/write their favourite AI response next to it.
  11. Close with a gallery walk or quick share-out: students show their "before" (Level 1) and "after" (Level 3) prompts to a partner and explain what changed.

Example Outputs

  • Level 1 prompt: "Help me plan a party." → Generic bullet list of party ideas with no context.
    Level 3 prompt: "You are an event planner. Plan a budget-friendly 12th birthday party for 15 kids in Nairobi, with an outdoor theme, under KES 5,000. Give me a table with activity, time, and cost." → A structured table with realistic local activities, timings, and costs.
  • Level 1 prompt: "Tell me about the water cycle." → A dense, textbook-style paragraph.
    Level 3 prompt: "You are a fun science teacher. Explain the water cycle to a 9-year-old using a short story about a raindrop named Dudu, in 5 sentences." → An engaging, age-appropriate mini-story that's easy to remember.
  • Level 1 prompt: "Give me a study plan." → Vague, one-size-fits-all list.
    Level 3 prompt: "You are a study coach. Create a 5-day revision timetable for a Grade 7 student preparing for a Maths exam on fractions and decimals, with 30-minute sessions and one fun break each day. Present it as a table." → A clear, personalized, actionable schedule.

Facilitation Tips

  • Pacing: Keep the first vague-prompt exercise short (under 5 minutes) — its purpose is just to create the "aha, that's not very useful" moment, not to analyze deeply.
  • Common confusion: Students often think longer prompts automatically mean better answers. Clarify that specificity, not length, is the key — a short but precise prompt beats a long rambling one.
  • Some students will get an unexpectedly poor or off-topic response even with a good prompt. Use this as a teaching moment: "AI doesn't always get it right first time — what could we add or change to fix this?" Encourage iterating rather than giving up.
  • Watch for students copying a classmate's exact prompt instead of writing their own — walk around and prompt them to personalize the topic.
  • If the free tool is slow or down, pair students up to share one working device rather than stalling the whole class.
  • Remind students that any personal information typed into the chat isn't private — avoid entering real names, addresses, or school details in prompts.
  • For younger or less confident writers, provide the Recipe Card as fill-in-the-blank sentence starters rather than a blank table.

Discussion Questions

  • What is the difference between a "vague" prompt and a "specific" prompt? Can you give an example of each?
  • Why do you think giving the AI a "role" (like "you are a vet" or "you are a teacher") changes its answer?
  • Was there ever a moment when a more detailed prompt still gave you a wrong or unhelpful answer? What did you do next?
  • Do you think there's such a thing as a prompt that's "too detailed" or "too long"? Why or why not?
  • How is asking a good question to an AI similar to or different from asking a good question to a teacher or friend?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Take one of your Level 3 prompts and change only the format instruction (e.g. ask for a poem instead of a list). Compare how differently the same information is presented.
  • Medium: Write a prompt that asks the AI to give you its answer in two different styles at once (e.g. "Explain this first like I'm 5 years old, then like I'm 15 years old") and compare the two explanations.
  • Hard: Design a "prompt chain" — a sequence of 3 connected prompts where each one builds on the AI's previous answer (e.g. first ask for a story idea, then ask it to turn that idea into a script, then ask it to suggest a title and moral). Present your final result and explain how each prompt shaped the next.
